title: Rubio’s speech: You can’t be grateful for what you can’t name October 25, 2026
author: Gary Houchens
source: Gary Houchens (garyhouchens.substack.com), column for the Bowling Green Daily News,
summary: Gary Houchens, an education professor writing in his regular newspaper column, uses Secretary of State Marco Rubio's October speech in Athens as a prompt for an argument about what schools owe students. Rubio described the freedom and prosperity of the modern West as an inheritance from Greece, Rome and Jerusalem rather than an accident, and Houchens adds historian Wilfred McClay's point that the Jewish and Christian tradition supplied the dignity of the person behind human rights. His claim is that young people enjoy these goods without knowing their sources, and that you cannot be grateful for or even intelligently critical of what you cannot name. The remedy he proposes is a return to classical sources and techniques, including the Great Books, the great conversation about a flourishing life, and the explicit formation of character. He rejects the idea that this means uncritical acceptance, citing Martin Luther King Jr.'s Letter from Birmingham Jail as a model of reform that works by recalling foundational ideals. He closes by pointing to the Phoenix Declaration, which he helped draft, as a practical roadmap.
points: Houchens argues that a civilisational inheritance has to be taught on purpose, so renewal depends on classrooms rather than on speeches.
His central claim is that gratitude and critique come from the same knowledge, which means students who cannot name the sources of their freedoms can neither appreciate nor responsibly reform them.
He prescribes classical sources and techniques, namely the Great Books, the great conversation and deliberate character formation, as the best strategy for passing the inheritance on.

Martin Luther King Jr. serves as his proof that deep knowledge of the tradition equips reformers, since King cited Socrates, Augustine, Aquinas and the Hebrew prophets while calling America back to its ideals.
He offers concrete steps from the Phoenix Declaration: reading primary sources, teaching founding documents alongside how the nation failed them, and tracing modern liberties to their origins.
quotes: According to Rubio, the freedom and prosperity that we enjoy today, unprecedented in human history, are an inheritance, not an accident. Generations from a multitude of cultural backgrounds have built upon that inheritance to bring us a civilization we increasingly take for granted.
From my perspective as an educator, this inheritance must be taught on purpose, and that is the work not only of great speeches but of schools.
You can’t be grateful for, or even appropriately critical of, things you cannot name. Gratitude and critique come from the same knowledge of the world around you. And this is a problem for schools.

The best strategy for schools to effectively pass down knowledge of this political, economic, and cultural inheritance is to return to classical sources and techniques of education. Schools should engage students with the Great Books, the works that made the modern world, and invite them into the great conversation, going on since the time of the ancient Greeks, about what it means to live a flourishing life.

None of this means blind acceptance of the world as it is, or a refusal to reform it. To the contrary, empowering students with a deep knowledge of the past, and how it shapes the contemporary world, not only fosters appreciation on the part of students, but also effectively equips them to critique both past and present.

King remade America precisely by recalling its foundational ideals and aspirations. In “Letter from Birmingham Jail,” King cited Socrates, Augustine and Aquinas, the Hebrew prophets, and the Declaration of Independence.

Any school can readily adopt some of the Phoenix Declaration’s key recommendations, including asking students to read primary sources, teaching American founding documents alongside examples of how we’ve failed to live up to their ideals, and helping students trace modern liberties back to their historical and philosophical origins.
